Salesforce Agentforce & AI Research October 8, 2026 Abstract We present Salesforce Koa, an enterprise language model built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-3-Super-120B foundation model with reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and deployed in FP8 for production. Koa is trained only on public and synthetically generated data, and specialized for the agentic tool use that enterprise workflows demand: routing a request to the correct action, invoking the right tool with valid arguments, and completing multi-turn business tasks. The distinctive component of our pipeline is specification-driven task construction: declarative Agent Script specifications are expanded into persona-conditioned multi-turn environments whose rewards are grounded in successful tool use. Applied to enterprise CRM specifications, the same pipeline produces the in-domain training distribution on which Koa is specialized. On CRMAgentBench and the human-labeled production tool-calling set, Koa outperforms both its untuned open-weight base and GPT-4.1 and is competitive with the strongest frontier models. It reaches 87% Task Success Rate on CRMAgentBench (vs. GPT-4.1 at 82% and the base at 79%), is at or near the top of every metric on the human-labeled portion of an internal production benchmark, and preserves the base model’s general capability on public benchmarks (Tau2Bench, BFCL). A controlled comparison with architecture and RL recipe held fixed shows that the additional in-domain RL stage improves argument accuracy and full tool-call success on the human-labeled enterprise benchmark. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) increasingly power enterprise AI systems, where, unlike general-purpose assistants, they must invoke external tools, retrieve structured information, and complete multi-step workflows across business applications. Robust tool use and agentic reasoning are therefore the essential enterprise capabilities. Many production systems rely on proprietary frontier models, yet enterprises often need more control over deployment, customization, governance, and cost than a single external provider allows. Recent open-weight foundation models such as Llama [ 7 ] , Gemma [ 8 ] , Qwen [ 27 ] , Mistral [ 11 ] , and Nemotron [ 13 ] have closed much of the public-benchmark gap, and access to weights lets organizations post-train for their own domains. A central question is whether they can be effectively specialized for enterprise agentic tasks while preserving general-purpose capability, and, if so, what matters most in doing so. We introduce Salesforce Koa, an enterprise language model built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-3-Super-120B foundation model (Nemotron-120B) with GRPO, using only public and synthetically generated data, and served in FP8 for production. The distinctive component of our pipeline is specification-driven task construction: for enterprise domains we build training tasks from declarative agent specifications written in Agent Script [ 23 ] , Salesforce’s declarative language for Agentforce agents. A specification captures an agent’s routing structure, subagents, typed actions, tool scopes, and workflow instructions; a simulation pipeline expands it into scenario- and persona-conditioned tasks that NeMo Gym [ 14 ] executes as online rollouts, with grounded task-resolution rewards driving GRPO. This creates a direct bridge between agent authoring and model post-training: the same specifications that configure an agent also structure its rollout tasks and resolution criteria. We organize the paper around the progression that produced Koa: from the untuned base, to RL on public and synthetic multi-domain data, to RL on the in-domain Salesforce distribution, to the FP8 model we deploy. RL on public and synthetic data yields modest gains on public benchmarks. Continuing training on the in-domain Salesforce distribution, with architecture and RL recipe held fixed, further improves argument accuracy and full tool-call success on the human-labeled enterprise benchmark. FP8 quantization yields comparable aggregate benchmark performance while making the 120B model efficient to serve. Because Koa is specialized for a specific production distribution, we evaluate it primarily on that distribution: we lead with enterprise benchmarks that reflect enterprise workflows—CRMAgentBench and a production tool-calling benchmark—and use public tool-calling benchmarks such as BFCL [ 17 ] as a check that general-purpose capability is preserved. Reporting both lets us separate what enterprise specialization changes on the deployment distribution from what it changes on generalist tasks. Our contributions are as follows. First, we present Koa, an enterprise model post-trained from the open-weight Nemotron-120B base with a specification-driven, simulation-to-reward RL pipeline and deployed in FP8; on CRMAgentBench it reaches 87% Task Success Rate, surpassing GPT-4.1 (82%) and the untuned Nemotron base (79%) and matching Nemotron-Ultra-550B, and on the human-labeled set of an internal production tool-calling benchmark it achieves the highest non-hallucination rate of any model evaluated and higher tool-name accuracy than all evaluated open-weight baselines. Second, holding architecture and RL recipe fixed, we compare the public-data RL checkpoint with the checkpoint obtained through additional in-domain RL, showing improved argument accuracy and full tool-call success on the human-labeled enterprise benchmark. Third, we provide a capability-preservation analysis on public benchmarks, including a per-subset account of a small BFCL change. Finally, we report a deployment study showing that FP8 quantization with in-domain calibration retains comparable aggregate benchmark performance for efficient 120B serving. 2 Related Work Open-weight foundation models. Recent advances in open-weight foundation models have substantially narrowed the gap with proprietary frontier models across reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks. Model families such as Llama [ 7 ] , Gemma [ 8 ] , Qwen [ 27 ] , Mistral [ 11 ] , and Nemotron [ 13 ] show that open weights provide a strong foundation for downstream adaptation, letting organizations post-train on their own data while retaining control over deployment and customization. We build on an open-weight Nemotron foundation model and study reinforcement learning as a mechanism for enterprise specialization. Enterprise language models and tool use. LLMs are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external tools rather than only generating text. Toolformer [ 24 ] , Gorilla [ 16 ] , and ToolLLM [ 20 ] demonstrate API invocation, function calling, and tool use, and benchmarks such as BFCL [ 17 ] , CRMArena [ 10 ] , and LoCoBench-Agent [ 21 ] establish tool use and agentic reasoning as critical capabilities. A complementary line of work builds large action models together with the data and tooling to train them: xLAM [ 31 ] trains open action-model families for agentic tasks; APIGen [ 12 ] and APIGen-MT [ 18 ] synthesize verifiable function-calling and multi-turn agent data; ActionStudio [ 30 ] provides a lightweight training framework for such models; and ToolLibGen [ 29 ] automatically creates and aggregates tool libraries. Enterprise applications place unique demands on these capabilities: rather than answering standalone questions, enterprise agents must retrieve structured information, invoke business APIs, and execute multi-step workflows over organization-specific schemas and policies, where tools may have overlapping functionality and an incorrect action can affect live business records. We focus on this enterprise setting and study how RL specializes an open-weight model for it, evaluating on both public function-calling benchmarks and enterprise CRM tasks. Post-training for LLMs. Post-training is a critical stage in building capable models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts foundation models to downstream tasks and improves instruction following [ 15 ] , while reinforcement learning—from RLHF and Constitutional AI [ 3 ] to policy-gradient methods such as PPO [ 25 ] and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [ 26 , 9 ] , preference optimization [ 22 ] , and on-policy distillation [ 2 ] —further improves reasoning and decision-making. A growing body of work continues to scale and specialize RL post-training [ 5 , 19 ] . Turn-local RL methods focus updates on selected agent decisions. PivotRL [ 28 ] filters intermediate turns from expert trajectories using verifier reward statistics and performs local RL updates. Critical-State RL [ 6 ] checks reward alignment and improvement headroom, separates action-dependent reward variation from continuation noise through nested sampling, and trains the selected model calls. We study post-training for enterprise adaptation from an already post-trained open-weight foundation model, comparing SFT and RL and, more centrally, isolating the effect of training on the deployment distribution. Our results show that additional in-domain RL improves argument accuracy and full tool-call success on the human-labeled enterprise benchmark. 3 Method Salesforce Koa is built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-120B foundation model with GRPO. Training uses only public resources and synthetically generated interactions. The distinctive component of our pipeline is specification-driven task construction : declarative enterprise agent specifications are expanded into executable, persona-conditioned multi-turn environments whose rewards are grounded in successful tool use; instantiated on production Salesforce specifications, the same construction yields the in-domain distribution on which Koa is specialized. We describe environment and task construction (Section 3.1 ), online rollout and the grounded reward (Section 3.2 ), policy optimization (Section 3.3 ), the training-data regimes that define our central comparison (Section 3.4 ), and FP8 quantization for deployment (Section 3.5 ). We apply RL directly to the base model rather than to an SFT checkpoint; a preliminary SFT study that motivated this choice, together with distributed-training and evaluation details, is deferred to Appendix C.1 and B.3 . 3.1 Spec-driven environment and task construction For enterprise domains, we author workflow structure in Agent Script. A specification defines a router, specialized subagents, typed actions, and natural-language reasoning instructions, which together determine how requests are routed, which tools are exposed within each topic, and how each topic handles its workflow. A static extraction pass compiles this specification into a typed workflow graph capturing per-tool argument schemas, declared state effects, routing conditions, and loop/termination configuration; this graph instantiates the executable environment, including the simulated state that tools read and mutate. For public tool-use domains, where no Agent Script specification exists, we instead synthesize the workflow structure directly, producing the same typed workflow graph of tools, argument schemas, and termination conditions; both sources therefore feed the shared simulation and reward machinery below equally. A simulation pipeline expands each specification into scenario- and persona-conditioned sessions: the scenario determines the workflows and user needs exercised, while the persona conditions the simulated customer’s behavior. These sessions are converted into RL examples that begin either from the opening request or from a generated dialogue prefix, exposing the policy to decisions at different depths of a multi-turn interaction. Each example uses a common schema in which agent_ref selects the environment and the remaining fields provide the initial rollout context (task intent, persona, dialogue state, available tools); the full trajectory is generated online. When multiple environments are trained jointly, per-row agent_ref dispatch lets a single run load them all, and differential exposure is realized by repeating an environment’s examples before shuffling. NeMo Gym then executes each example as an online rollout, so workflow authoring and task construction are cleanly separated from rollout execution and policy optimization. 3.2 Online rollout and grounded reward Each example is executed inside a NeMo Gym environment. For simulated-dialogue environments a single frozen helper model plays three roles in every rollout: a customer simulator (produces the next user turn from the sampled persona), a tool/function emulator (produces tool outputs when no production backend exists), and a coverage judge (scores resolution to form the reward). The helper is a separate inference service and is never updated by policy optimization. Figure 1 in Appendix A.2 traces one rollout end to end, making explicit which components are frozen versus trained, the order of interactions within a turn, and where the scalar reward comes from. The reward is built from the coverage judge. The task intent is represented as numbered sub-questions, and the judge emits one resolved/not-resolved verdict per sub-question over the full transcript. The coverage rate is cov = # ​ { sub-questions judged resolved } # ​ { sub-questions } ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \mathrm{cov}=\frac{\#\{\text{sub-questions judged resolved}\}}{\#\{\text{sub-questions}\}}\in[0,1], (1) where missing or malformed verdicts default to not resolved. The scalar reward applies a duplicate-call gate, R = { 0 , a consecutive duplicate tool call occurred, cov , otherwise, R=\begin{cases}0,&\text{a consecutive duplicate tool call occurred,}\\ \mathrm{cov},&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (2) and the judge prompt requires that any sub-question needing customer- or system-specific data be marked resolved only when the answer is grounded in a successful relevant tool call; generic factoids may resolve without a tool. The deterministic sandbox environment instead sets R = 1 R=1 exactly when the predicted actions reproduce the reference end state and R = 0 R=0 otherwise. This grounding is deliberate: it rewards the model for acting through the right tool, the behavior enterprise workflows require, and—as we discuss in Section 5 —also shapes which public-benchmark categories move after specialization. A few properties of these environments are central to their behavior. The tool list is per rollout, not global: each conversation advertises only the tools available in its source session, and in routed environments the visible set is further restricted to the active subagent, so the policy sees only in-scope tools at any moment. Task intent is constructed deterministically at build time (a numbered list of sub-questions), directly connecting task construction to the reward. A persona is sampled per conversation and held constant, controlling how the simulated user reacts, escalates, or declares resolution. Focus system prompts are not restricted to the conversation start: in routed environments each subagent switch appends a fresh focus/procedure message, re-focusing the policy exactly when the topic changes. Environments differ mainly in interaction topology and verification (Appendix A.1 , Table 8 ). 3.3 Optimization We maximize the expected trajectory reward 𝒥 ( θ ) = 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒟 𝔼 τ ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , env ) [ R ( τ ) ] \mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\mathrm{env})}[R(\tau)] with GRPO variants: For each prompt the policy samples a small group of complete trajectories with colocated inference; dynamic sampling discards zero-variance groups and refills until a full batch is assembled. Advantages are estimated by a leave-one-out group baseline (no value network), and a token-level truncated importance-sampling weight corrects the train/generation log-probability mismatch under a single on-policy update per batch. Trajectories with malformed tool-call or thinking syntax have the offending token advantages set to a fixed negative value, and over-length or log-probability-inconsistent trajectories are masked. The full objective, advantage normalization, and validity constraints are given in Appendix B.1 . A complementary single-step training mode for constrained decision turns, which isolates the rare but decisive turns where the agent must communicate with the user rather than call a tool, is described in Appendix B.2 . 3.4 Training-data regimes Koa is produced by two RL stages on data from different regimes, applied in sequence from the Nemotron base, with the RL recipe of Sections 3.2 – 3.3 held fixed throughout. The first stage uses the public / synthetic regime, which generates rollouts against multi-domain environments ( salesforce support , healthcare administration , real estate , and a helper-free workplace assistant sandbox) built from public tool schemas and synthesized workflow structure, measuring how far a general spec-driven recipe carries on public benchmarks. We then continue training with a second stage on the in-domain Salesforce regime, which instantiates the same spec-driven construction (Section 3.1 ) on production Salesforce agent specifications and tool schemas, so that the synthesized sessions’ tool inventories, argument conventions, and multi-turn workflows match the production distribution the model will serve; as in the public/synthetic regime, it uses only specification-derived and synthesized interactions. This in-domain stage produces the deployed Koa checkpoint. Because the base and RL recipe are held fixed and the only change is the added in-domain stage, the improvement on the production distribution is attributable to in-domain adaptation. Section 4.2 reports the controlled result; Section 5 discusses the effects of in-domain adaptation and FP8 deployment. 3.5 FP8 quantization for deployment The deployed Koa checkpoint is served in FP8 for inference efficiency. We apply post-training quantization (PTQ) with NVIDIA ModelOpt, using in-domain calibration data drawn from the production distribution rather than generic calibration text, so that quantization statistics reflect the tool-calling traffic the model actually serves. We refer to the unquantized checkpoint as Koa (BF16) and the deployed model as Koa (FP8) , and report both so the effect of quantization can be isolated (Section 5 ). 4 Experiments We post-train the Nemotron-3-Super-120B policy on multi-domain agentic tool-calling tasks and evaluate it against strong open and proprietary baselines. Consistent with the motivation in Section 2 , we lead with enterprise benchmarks (Section 4.2 ), which reflect the production distribution Koa is built to serve, and then report public benchmarks (Section 4.3 ) as a check that general capability is preserved. 4.1 Setup Policies and helper. Both trained policies are Nemotron reasoning models run in thinking mode. The Nemotron-3-Super-120B is the final target policy; a Nano v3 ( ∼ \sim 30B) model served as a cheap proxy on which we developed the GRPO reward/algorithm recipe before porting it to the 120B policy, and the same Nano-30B runs inside the environments as the frozen helper that plays customer simulator, tool emulator, and coverage judge. Full infrastructure details are in Appendix B.3 . Baselines. We compare Koa with two proprietary frontier models (GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.5) and with its open-weight base, Nemotron-3-Super-120B, focusing on models evaluated on our production benchmark; CRMAgentBench adds Gemini and Nemotron-Ultra-550B for context. GPT-4.1 and the untuned Nemotron base are the two references we care most about: GPT-4.1 is a widely deployed proprietary baseline, and the untuned base isolates the effect of our post-training. Serving and precision. We serve Nemotron and our fine-tuned checkpoints via vLLM with tensor parallelism, supporting up to 256K context. These checkpoints are evaluated in BF16, except the production Koa model, which is served in FP8 for inference efficiency; the corresponding BF16 checkpoint is reported as Koa (BF16) to isolate the effect of quantization. 4.2 Enterprise benchmark results We evaluate on three enterprise benchmarks, each targeting CRM agent behavior from a different angle: CRMAgentBench , a multi-domain, multi-turn agent benchmark scored by end-to-end task success; a production tool-calling benchmark —an internal set with human-labeled and synthetic splits—which gives our most decisive, controlled result; and CRM Bench , a multi-dimensional assessment of single-turn CRM assistant behavior (reported with the public benchmarks in Section 4.3 , Table 6 ). 4.2.1 CRMAgentBench CRMAgentBench is a multi-node ReAct agent framework with an integrated benchmark suite. It ships five production-style CRM agents—Customer Service, Store Manager, Field Service, Sales Development Rep (SDR), and Marketing—spanning 97 tasks. Each task is run as a full multi-turn conversation between two language models: an LLM user simulator that plays the customer from a scripted persona, and the agent under test. Tools are stateful, reading and writing a shared mock database, so the benchmark verifies the agent’s side effects rather than only its final message. The headline metric is Task Success Rate (TSR), a strict, all-or-nothing pass per task: a task counts as solved only when all of its asserted checks hold (actions taken, resulting state, tool arguments, response content and order, and avoidance of forbidden actions). We report TSR overall (pooled across all 97 tasks) and per domain. As shown in Table 1 , Koa reaches 87% overall TSR, clearly above GPT-4.1 (82%) and its untuned Nemotron base (79%), and matching Nemotron-Ultra-550B despite being far smaller. Koa trails the strongest generalists (GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, both 91%) by a modest margin. The gains over the base are largest in Field Service ( 74 → 91 74\to 91 ) and Store Manager ( 76 → 86 76\to 86 ). 4.2.2 Production tool-calling benchmark We benchmark the production model against frontier and open baselines on two in-house evaluation sets: an internal human-labeled set and an internal synthetic set judged by multiple LLMs. The production Koa model is our single-environment RL checkpoint (step 100) after FP8 post-training quantization. Metrics are tool-name accuracy ( Name ), LLM-judged argument accuracy ( Args ), full tool-call success with both name and arguments correct ( Succ ), and the non-hallucination rate ( NoHall , predicted function within the allowed set); higher is better throughout. We present two views of the same benchmark: Table 2 places Koa against frontier and open baselines, and Table 3 isolates the effect of training data and precision with architecture and recipe held fixed. On the human-labeled set in Table 2 , Koa outperforms GPT-4.1 on all four metrics. It achieves the highest non-hallucination rate of any model (0.989), higher tool-name accuracy than all evaluated open-weight baselines (0.966), and argument and success scores (0.851/0.848) ahead of GPT-5.5 and both Gemini models. On the synthetic set the frontier models lead on success (GPT-5.5 0.902, GPT-4.1 0.897) while Koa scores 0.847. The training-data and precision ablation in Table 3 holds architecture and recipe fixed to isolate in-domain RL and FP8 quantization; we analyze it in Section 5 . With the base and RL recipe held fixed, the added in-domain stage is the only difference. On the human-labeled enterprise benchmark, this in-domain stage improves success and argument accuracy from 0.825 / 0.825 0.825/0.825 to 0.842 / 0.842 0.842/0.842 , and Salesforce Koa reaches 0.848 / 0.851 0.848/0.851 . 5.2 SFT versus RL from an already post-trained base A natural alternative to RL is supervised fine-tuning. Starting from the same post-trained Nemotron base, we compare SFT-only and RL-only checkpoints, with the Tau2Bench, BFCL, and CRM Bench breakdowns in Appendix C (Tables 9 – 11 ). On Tau2Bench both improve modestly over the base (SFT 70.04, RL 69.41, base 68.64), with SFT strongest by a small margin. The clear distinction is on BFCL multi-turn tool use: SFT slightly reduces accuracy ( → 53.25 54.12\!\to\!53.25 ) whereas RL improves it substantially to 59.50 59.50 , and SFT’s gains concentrate in memory and relevance detection that do not transfer to multi-turn performance. On the predominantly single-turn CRM Bench, SFT is effective ( → 0.88 0.84\!\to\!0.88 ), edging RL ( 0.86 0.86 ). Because enterprise workflows are multi-turn, we choose RL over SFT as the adaptation method . The deployed Koa applies this RL recipe in two stages, public/synthetic followed by in-domain Salesforce (Section 5.1 ), and is served in FP8; the RL-only checkpoint here isolates the method choice against SFT. We treat this comparison as scoped to a base that is itself already RL-post-trained, since from a pre-RL checkpoint the conclusion could differ. 5.3 General tool use across our checkpoints and FP8 deployment Table 7: BFCL across Koa’s two-stage RL pipeline: the Nemotron-3-Super-120B base, a first RL stage on public/synthetic data, a second RL stage on enterprise data (Koa), and FP8 deployment. The first stage, RL on the public/synthetic regime, scores highest on BFCL, above the Nemotron base ( 66.63 66.63 vs. 64.73 64.73 ), with its largest gains on multi-turn tool use ( → 59.50 54.12\!\to\!59.50 ) and web search ( → 73.50 71.50\!\to\!73.50 ); the spec-driven recipe generalizes well on public agentic tasks. BFCL peaks on the public regime, whereas the deployed model optimizes the in-domain distribution that drives enterprise value, holding parity with its base on public tool use while leading where deployment matters. 6 Conclusion We presented Salesforce Koa, an enterprise language model built by post-training the open-weight Nemotron-120B foundation model with GRPO and deployed in FP8. On CRMAgentBench and the human-labeled production tool-calling set, Koa outperforms both its untuned open-weight base and GPT-4.1 and is competitive with the strongest frontier models, while preserving general tool-use capability on public benchmarks. Its central contribution is a specification-driven RL pipeline in which the same declarative Agent Script specifications that configure an agent also supply the workflow structure and grounded rewards for its rollout tasks; instantiated on enterprise CRM specifications, this yields the in-domain distribution on which Koa is specialized. Our controlled comparison shows that, with architecture and RL recipe held fixed, an additional in-domain RL stage improves argument accuracy and full tool-call success on the human-labeled enterprise benchmark. Two limitations temper these results: our base is itself already RL-post-trained, so the preference for RL over SFT may not hold from a pre-RL checkpoint, and some enterprise evaluations use modest task counts. Future work includes co-designing the SFT and RL stages, evaluating from a pre-RL foundation, and extending specification-driven environments to broader domains and more complex agentic workflows. 7 Acknowledgements This model was trained in partnership with NVIDIA. A complementary single-step mode for constrained decision turns (Appendix B.2 ) targets turns where the agent must communicate with the user rather than call a tool. B.2 Constrained decision turns A complementary training mode targets constrained decision turns , where the agent cannot resolve a request through tool execution alone and must instead interact with the user (communicate a limitation, request missing information, or manage expectations). We create the constraint dynamically by withholding a needed tool at a designated turn while the simulated customer issues a request that requires it. We form a single prompt-response training row at that turn. The single-step reward follows the same gate-then-score pattern as Eq. 2 : a procedural gate zeroes the reward on any premature state-changing call, and a consequence score grades whether the withheld tool is correctly emitted at a later recovery turn (generated only for reward computation and excluded from the gradient) [ 6 ] . These rows are trained with the same GRPO optimizer (Eq. 3 ); the environment builder produces both turn-0 and mid-conversation constrained states. B.3 Distributed training and offline evaluation Policy training is distributed with tensor, expert, and sequence parallelism (TP=8, EP=8, PP=1); rollout generation runs colocated on the actor workers, alternating generation and optimization. The frozen environment helper is served as a single separate inference engine to avoid a data-parallel coordination failure mode observed when the helper was split across replicas. Single-env GRPO uses 4 actor nodes (32 B200s, DP=4) plus 1 dedicated helper node (8 B200s, TP=8); multi-env GRPO uses the same layout. During training, validation replays held-out environment examples and reports aggregate and per-environment reward. Offline evaluation is kept independent of the training-time helper: checkpoints are served under greedy decoding, tool calls are parsed with a schema-aware parser, and tool-name, argument, and full-call correctness are scored, including an independent LLM judge for argument equivalence. Appendix C Additional post-training experiments C.1 Preliminary SFT setup We ran a preliminary SFT study on the already post-trained Nemotron base using a masked next-token loss restricted to target (assistant and tool-call) tokens. The entire corpus is synthetic, generated with a pipeline built on APIGen [ 12 ] and APIGen-MT [ 18 ] , using only publicly available function-calling resources (tool collections from BFCL [ 17 ] and Tau2Bench Airline [ 4 ] ) as schemas and executable environments. We perform full-parameter fine-tuning of Nemotron-120B with NeMo Automodel [ 1 ] over 32 H200 GPUs (FSDP2, expert parallelism, activation checkpointing) at sequence length 8192 8192 and global batch size 32 32 , with a deliberately conservative recipe (peak learning rate 5 × 10 − 8 5\times 10^{-8} , cosine decay, gradient clipping, early stopping) to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
